what: An API gateway is the single front door to many backend services. It checks who is calling, slows down callers who send too much, and sends each request to the right service.
like: Like a hotel reception desk: it checks your booking, hands out keys, and points you to the right room, so guests never wander the corridors alone.
why: One public address for many services, so clients never need to know your internal layout
Shared jobs done once: auth, throttling, caching, logging and request reshaping
Safe releases: send a small slice of traffic to a new version first (a canary)

nodes.t: Auth check|verify JWT or API key
Response cache|GET only, with a TTL

steps.d: Every client calls one address, like api.shop.com. The gateway ends the HTTPS connection (TLS termination) and handles the request before any backend sees it.
The gateway checks the token: a JWT (a signed JSON pass) has its signature and expiry (exp) verified, or an API key is looked up. Bad tokens never reach a service.
Each caller gets a token bucket: a steady refill rate plus a burst allowance. An empty bucket means the gateway replies 429 Too Many Requests and the caller retries later.
Routing rules match the path, host or a header and forward to the right service. The gateway can rewrite the URL, add or strip headers, and reshape the body on the way.
For repeat GET requests the gateway can keep the response for a TTL (time to live). A cache hit returns at once and the backend does no work.
A weighted rule sends, say, 5% of traffic to a canary. If its errors and latency look good you promote it; if not, you set it back to 0%.

choices.d: Managed (AWS API Gateway, Azure API Management) means no servers to run. Self-run (Kong, Envoy) gives full control and no vendor quotas, but you operate and scale it.
Verify tokens at the gateway so services trust one checked identity. Services still check permissions for their own data (authorization), since the gateway only knows who you are.
Limit per API key, user or IP. Counters kept on each node are fast but drift as you add nodes; a shared store like Redis keeps every node's count accurate.
Set a timeout per route and retry only safe, idempotent calls (ones you can repeat without harm). Long jobs belong in a queue, not a waiting HTTP call.

choices.t: One gateway or a BFF per app
choices.d: One shared gateway for common jobs. Add a BFF (backend for frontend) per client type when web and mobile need very different response shapes.

instead.why: Just spreads traffic over copies of one service, no auth or API keys
Only throttling, as a small focused piece you can place anywhere
Caches files close to users worldwide, before traffic reaches the gateway

breaks.d: Every request passes through the gateway, so a single small instance limits the whole system.
breaks.see: Gateway CPU high and p99 latency (the slowest 1 in 100 requests) rising while services look calm
breaks.fix: Keep the gateway stateless and run several copies across zones behind a load balancer, with autoscaling

breaks.d: One busy client uses up a shared account limit, so other callers get throttled too.
breaks.see: 429 Too Many Requests across many APIs while backends are idle
breaks.fix: Per-client limits and quotas (usage plans), a higher account quota, and client retries with backoff plus jitter

breaks.d: A backend takes longer than the gateway is willing to wait.
breaks.see: 504 Gateway Timeout on reports or exports, often at the same duration each time
breaks.fix: Return 202 Accepted with a job id, do the work from a queue, and let the client poll or get a push

breaks.d: Each gateway node counts on its own, so a client spread across nodes gets more than its limit.
breaks.see: A client's real rate is several times its configured limit
breaks.fix: Share counters in Redis, or put a consistent-hashing load balancer in front so a client sticks to one node

breaks.d: Feature rules get added to the gateway until every release needs a gateway change.
breaks.see: Most deploys touch gateway config; one team becomes a bottleneck
breaks.fix: Keep the gateway to shared jobs; move client-specific shaping into a BFF and rules into services

say: I'll put an API gateway in front of the services so clients have one address, and it handles TLS, JWT checks and per-key rate limits in one place.
Routing is by path, so /users goes to the users service and /orders to the orders service, and the gateway can split traffic by weight for canary releases.
The gateway stays stateless and runs as several copies behind a load balancer, with rate limit counters shared in Redis so limits stay accurate.
If web and mobile need very different payloads, I'd add a thin BFF per client behind the gateway rather than piling that logic into the gateway.

followups.q: How is a gateway different from a load balancer and a service mesh?
followups.a: A load balancer spreads traffic over copies of one service. A gateway is the front door for outside callers, adding auth, API keys, throttling and routing to many services. A service mesh, often built on Envoy sidecars, handles service-to-service traffic inside the system.

followups.q: Should services trust the gateway completely?
followups.a: Trust it for identity, since it verified the token. Each service still checks what that caller may do with its own data, and services should only accept traffic from the gateway or the mesh.

followups.q: How do you rate limit across 10 gateway nodes?
followups.a: Keep counters in a shared store like Redis so every node sees the same count, or route each client to the same node. Purely local counters are fastest but let a client exceed its limit.

followups.q: When would you add a BFF?
followups.a: When different clients need different data shapes, like a slim mobile payload and a rich web page. Each frontend team owns its BFF. Skip it when all clients make similar calls, since it adds a hop and some duplicated code.

today: Gateways now front AI models too: Azure API Management's AI gateway can cap LLM tokens per minute per caller, cache similar prompts and spread load across model backends.

check.q: A client sends too many requests and the gateway throttles it. Which status code comes back?
check.why: 429 means slow down and retry later. 401 is for a missing or bad token.

check.q: Your gateway runs on 5 nodes and each keeps its own rate counters. What can happen?
check.a: A client can get more than its limit
check.why: Each node counts only its share. Shared counters (for example in Redis) fix it.

check.q: You want 5% of users on a new orders version first. Which gateway feature helps?
check.a: Weighted routing for a canary release
check.why: A weight sends a small slice of traffic to the new version so you can watch it before promoting.

check.q: Web and mobile need very different response shapes. What is a good pattern?
check.a: A backend for frontend (BFF) per client type
d: One huge gateway rule per screen
A separate DNS name per user
check.why: A BFF tailors data for one client and keeps that logic out of the shared gateway.
